questions.question: What is the University of Minnesota's current AI policy?
questions.answer: There is no single AI policy — there are several layers. In the classroom: each instructor sets the rules (the Provost provides template syllabus statements), but the default under the Student Conduct Code is that AI use on coursework without instructor authorization is scholastic dishonesty. For data: only Public-classified data may go into AI tools that aren't UMN-licensed; the licensed tools (Google Gemini, NotebookLM, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion) carry contractual data protections. UMN licenses no AI detector and recommends against using them. Governance is newly centralized: a Vice Provost for AI and a university-wide AI Hub, both created in March 2026.

sources.title: AI: Appropriate Use of Generative AI Tools — OIT

questions.question: Can I use ChatGPT (or other AI) on my homework?
questions.answer: It depends on your instructor. UMN has no university-wide classroom AI rule — each instructor sets their course's policy, usually in the syllabus. The default matters, though: the Student Conduct Code treats unauthorized use of 'online learning support platforms' (which includes generative AI) as scholastic dishonesty, so if your syllabus is silent, ask before using AI. Failing to disclose AI use when disclosure is required also counts.

sources.title: Avoiding Scholastic Dishonesty — Office for Community Standards

questions.question: What AI tools does UMN provide to students, faculty, and staff?
questions.answer: As of January 2026, UMN licenses four generative AI tools with contractual data protections: Google Gemini with enterprise-grade data protection (opt-in, 100 prompts/day, available since July 2025), Google NotebookLM, Microsoft Copilot Chat with Enterprise Data Protection (sign in with your UMN Internet ID), and Zoom AI Companion (opt-in). UMN has no institutional ChatGPT agreement — consumer ChatGPT accounts carry no UMN protections.

sources.title: Gemini with Enterprise-Grade Data Protection — IT@UMN

questions.question: What University data can I put into an AI tool?
questions.answer: It depends on the tool and the data's classification. Public data can go into any AI platform. Private-Restricted data (student grades, UCard numbers) and Private-Highly Restricted data (SSNs, medical records) may NOT be put into AI tools that aren't UMN-licensed — doing so violates University policy. Even in licensed tools, restrictions apply: PHI is no longer approved for Microsoft Copilot, for example.

sources.title: AI: Appropriate Use of Generative AI Tools — OIT

questions.question: Does UMN use AI detectors on student work?
questions.answer: No — not officially. UMN licenses no AI-detection tool, and Turnitin's AI Writing Indicator is explicitly not enabled for UMN. University guidance warns instructors that detectors are unreliable (false accusations, bias against non-native English writers) and that running student work through unvetted third-party detectors risks violating FERPA. That said, AI-related discipline still happens — a PhD student's 2025 expulsion over alleged AI use was upheld on appeal in 2026.

sources.title: What Faculty Should Know About GenAI Detectors — Teaching Support

questions.question: Who can see my data in Canvas?
questions.answer: Canvas (run by Instructure, procured through the Unizin consortium) is UMN's system of record for coursework and grades, which are FERPA-protected education records — accessible to school officials with a legitimate educational interest, such as your instructors and TAs. The contract's specific data-protection terms are not published; UMN is also a member of Unizin, whose data platform aggregates learning data across member universities under terms that are not publicly documented.

questions.question: Does UMN use exam proctoring software?
questions.answer: Yes. Since 2025 UMN uses Honorlock (which replaced Proctorio, used 2017–2025). Honorlock's AI flags suspicious behavior and can trigger a live human proctor; exams may include webcam recording and room scans. Per UMN, recordings are FERPA-protected, viewable only by UMN instructors/TAs/designated IT staff, and retained about one year; Honorlock staff lack access to personally identifiable information. Instructors must give written advance notice, and students consent at exam login. Respondus LockDown Browser also remains in use.

sources.title: Fall 2025 Academic Technology Tools Update — UMD ITSS
Online Assessments and e-Proctoring Guidance — Teaching Support

questions.question: Is my UMN email private? Does Google read it?
questions.answer: UMN email runs on Google Workspace under a negotiated contract that UMN says protects the privacy and confidentiality of student, faculty, staff, and alumni data — FERPA-protected data is permitted in core Google apps, and a HIPAA agreement covers health units. The full contract text is not published. Note that since 2024, UMN no longer provides email for life: alumni and retirees lose @umn.edu addresses.

sources.title: Google Apps: Acceptable Use and Data Security — IT@UMN

questions.question: How should I cite or disclose AI use in my work?
questions.answer: UMN Libraries' guidance: cite generative AI whenever you paraphrase, quote, or incorporate AI-generated text, images, data, or code; acknowledge functional uses (like editing your prose or translating) in a note; and follow your instructor's specific rules. Watch out for hallucinated citations — AI tools fabricate plausible-looking articles and page numbers. Copy-pasting AI output into an assignment without authorization is plagiarism under the Conduct Code.

sources.title: Generative AI tools — UMN Libraries research guide

questions.question: I'm an instructor — how do I set an AI policy for my course?
questions.answer: Use the Provost's GenAI syllabus statements, developed with the Senate Committee on Educational Policy: customizable templates ranging from 'no restrictions' to complete prohibition. Be explicit about which uses and which tools are allowed and how students must disclose AI assistance. UMN recommends pointing students to UMN-licensed tools (Gemini, Copilot), which are vetted for accessibility and data privacy — and recommends against relying on AI detectors.

sources.title: Teaching with Generative AI — Teaching Support

questions.question: Who is in charge of AI at UMN?
questions.answer: Since March 2026, Dr. Galin Jones is UMN's inaugural Vice Provost for Artificial Intelligence, leading the new university-wide AI Hub. That structure came out of the Presidential AI Task Force (charged January 2025), whose public reports recommended a central governance framework. Day-to-day rules still flow through existing offices: OIT (tools and data rules), the Provost (teaching guidance), and the Policy Library (formal policies).

questions.question: How does UMN compare with other Big Ten schools on AI?
questions.answer: UMN is mid-pack. Like every Big Ten school, it leaves classroom AI rules to instructors. On tools, UMN licenses Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot but — unlike ASU, UCLA, Illinois, or Nebraska — has no OpenAI deal, and unlike Michigan (U-M GPT) or Penn State (AI Studio), no homegrown AI platform. Ohio State's 'AI Fluency' graduation initiative and Purdue's AI competency requirement go further curricularly. UMN's distinctive moves: an explicit no-AI-detectors stance and new central governance (Vice Provost for AI, 2026).

questions.question: How much does UMN spend on ed tech contracts?
questions.answer: Nobody outside the administration knows the full total — most contract amounts are never disclosed. What is public comes from Board of Regents docket summaries (required only for purchases of $1,000,000+) and news reporting: roughly $10 million to Oracle for PeopleSoft licensing and maintenance (2025–2027), $7.29 million to Salesforce (2023–2028), a reported $5.02 million for Canvas via the Unizin consortium (2017–2022) plus about $427,500/year in Unizin membership fees, about $281,000/year for Zoom, and the one-time $83.5 million ESUP systems upgrade completed in 2015. Contracts under $1 million — Turnitin, Kaltura, Honorlock, Qualtrics, and many more — are not publicly reported at all.

sources.title: University continues use of Zoom amid questions about privacy — Minnesota Daily

questions.question: What student data does UMN share with ed tech vendors?
questions.answer: More than is publicly documented. Canvas holds coursework and grades — FERPA-protected records — on Instructure's servers, and UMN belongs to Unizin, whose data platform aggregates learning data across member universities under terms that are not public. Google hosts everyone's email and documents under a negotiated contract. Honorlock receives exam recordings including webcam video and room scans (retained about a year). Turnitin keeps submitted student papers in its comparison database. In most cases, the contracts defining exactly what data flows to vendors — and what vendors may do with it — are not published; UMN says FERPA protections apply, but verifying that independently requires a public-records request.

sources.title: Google Apps: Acceptable Use and Data Security — IT@UMN

questions.question: Why can't I read UMN's contracts with tech companies?
questions.answer: Because UMN doesn't publish them — and isn't required to. Purchases of $1,000,000+ appear only as one-paragraph summaries in Board of Regents docket PDFs (that's how the Oracle ~$10M and Salesforce $7.29M figures are public), and purchases of $5,000,000+ require Board approval. But full contract text is published nowhere, and there is no searchable contracts database. The remedy: as a public institution, UMN is subject to the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, so you can request the contract documents directly.

questions.question: Did UMN really invent part of the internet?
questions.answer: Yes — the Gopher protocol, released in April 1991 by Mark McCahill's team at UMN's Microcomputer Center and named for the Golden Gophers. For about two years it was the dominant way to navigate the internet, before losing out to the World Wide Web — a defeat hastened when UMN announced licensing fees in 1993, just as CERN made the Web free. The earliest known use of the phrase 'surfing the internet' on Usenet is McCahill's, describing Gopher.

sources.title: The rise and fall of the Gopher protocol — MinnPost

questions.question: Are my Zoom classes recorded, and is that private?
questions.answer: Instructors can record Zoom classes; recordings of class sessions that identify students are generally FERPA-protected education records. UMN licensed Zoom in January 2019 (reported ~$281,000/year), reviewed its contract and privacy terms before signing, and maintains a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement plus a separate health-care instance. Zoom AI Companion is available but off by default.

sources.title: University continues use of Zoom amid questions about privacy — Minnesota Daily

questions.question: Do UMN's technology choices have to be accessible?
questions.answer: Yes. UMN's digital accessibility policy requires digital content and IT — including purchased software and AI tools — to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA, with enforcement beginning April 26, 2027 under the ADA Title II web rule. There's also a 'Digital Accessibility in Procurement' procedure, one reason UMN steers people toward licensed AI tools that have been vetted for accessibility.

sources.title: Accessibility of Digital Content and IT — Policy Library
